title: As AI makes gamedev more accessible what genre or style of game you think will get more value?
author: FutureLynx_
selftext:
Imagine in like 10 years, the quantity of games we will have that are made at least partially by AI. At that point that will lower the value of these games if not by sheer amount of offer.

So the standards will rise and the value will shift towards something that is either harder to do or more rare...

This is hard to predict...Anyways, let me know what you thinkk

comments.author: affabledrunk
comments.body:
I think you'll see a lot more excellent indie style games because the technical bar is lowered so much that you don't have to be a super-code monkey to implement. There are people with great design ideas today that couldn't implement them.

I'm thinking mostly of rogue-likes since thats my bag. I think we'll get more games of the same caliber as FTL or Into The Breach.

replies.author: BAJ-JohnBen
replies.body:
>super-code monkey to implement.

  
Plenty of ways to create a game that doesn't require a lot of coding.

replies.author: affabledrunk
replies.body: Yes but even using frameworks like rpgmaker and godot get very complex if you’re not doing something trivial. Vibe-coding it is orders of magnitude less complex.

replies.author: BAJ-JohnBen
replies.body:
Game Maker and Construct, plenty more lowers the bar in terms of gaming. Game Maker's webstite state you can make a game in 15 minutes. Like, I was going to use Godot for a side-project of mine, but realized Game Maker is simpler engine for the idea I got in mind. 

RPGMaker and Godot aren't low code/no-code. RPGMaker lowers the bar a lot, but you still need to know what you're doing. Godot has positioned itself as the free/open-source Unity alt. 

Game dev isn't complex, just requires patience. The issue is, a lot of people don't have that and they want to make their flashy big game right off the bat.

replies.author: Nerodon
replies.body: I disagree with that statement... any sufficiently advanced game to surpass a trivial use case of Godot or RPGMaker will require excellent knowledge of application and game design even if the code is generated. If you didnt have the skill to write it without AI, I'm telling you, you're going to run into the wildest rabbit holes and hard walls all over the place and be ill equipped to pivot and progress.

comments.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
comments.body:
I think it will be as simple as the highest quality games will rise to the top and it won’t matter if ai was used or not. It’ll just be harder for people as a whole to find out which indie games are the highest quality because there will be way more games to pick thru. 

I also suspect the games that at least seem “handcrafted” will do better. People will grow more wary of stuff that looks like slop. Before it was asset flips and now it will be ai-slop.

Hidden gems will be harder to discover which will be a bummer.

I bet the number of AAA games using ai to some degree is already near 100%. Indies will see the struggle.

replies.author: Nerodon
replies.body:
100% real take...
When steam greenlight went away, hidden gems got buried, AI games flooding in will only make this worse and saturate and already saturated market with relatively low quality titles.

No rip on dev using AI to make high quality games... but you all know that's not gonna be your typical thing.

replies.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
replies.body: Maybe indie publishers will be more important and people won’t want to but self published games. Indie fans might want the Devolver badge of approval or something.

replies.author: Nerodon
replies.body: It's gonna be a battle for reputation and marketting rather than just ability to create a game

replies.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
replies.body: I agree. Doing this for fun but I do feel like I’m building something pretty good and I hate trying to market stuff 😖. I do feel like indie steam games would get recognized if they were an absolute banger in the past because people were just desperate to find hidden gems and eventually word would spread. I have a feeling like that might change.

replies.author: Disposable110
replies.body:
It's going to be like Youtube where everyone can suddenly be a youtuber as there is zero barrier to entry.

But 99.9% of the youtube vidoes do not get more than 10 views, and it's not exactly cream rising to the top, just luck and virality.

replies.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
replies.body:
Thinking a little more deeply I think you are somewhat right. 

Personally I think when a game is an absolute BANGER it will be discovered. I’m not talking about a game that’s just very good. I’m talking about a game that’s so appealing to either the masses or a niche community that one just a few people play it, it spreads by word and on internet. People will tell their friends.

I don’t see a world where a game like Celeste or Slay the Spire or something comes out and it’s just unknown. 

I do think very good hidden gems will get missed though 😔

replies.author: Disposable110
replies.body:
[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amulets\_%26\_Armor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amulets_%26_Armor)

\- Basically the definition of extraction shooter, in 1997

\- Full RPG + FPS gameplay

\- Multiplayer

\- Absolute metric ton of content

\- Competitive graphics for its time

\- Commercial flop with fewer than 100 units sold

\- Pretty likely the first time you heard of this game

replies.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
replies.body:
Maybe it’s an absolute banger. Haven’t played it. TBH it looks like something I would like. Almost 30 years ago though, different time. I don’t think word of a banger game would spread the same way it does now just with how the internet was and that most people didn’t have the internet.

And if you wanted the game you’d usually have to find it on a shelf at a store you couldn’t just download it. Maybe you could order it from the publishers website.

replies.author: Disposable110
replies.body: Give it a go, there's a windows version around nowadays. Controls and responsiveness is a bit rough in this day and age, but all the other mechanics that were outlandish, new and weird at the time are now mainstream features.

comments.author: count023
comments.body: ones made by the Autuer, like Undertale or Balatro. Gimmicky ideas that will have \_zero\_ mainstream appeal so they wont get any funding or pick up by a studio, but one little guy with a brainworm about a crazy idea will have great success if they can put their pent opaper, as it were.

replies.author: Nerodon
replies.body:
The science behind viral titles is unknown, even without AI, it's always impossible to predict which new game will be a hit.

You can't assume that because in theory, those game could have been made by AI, that viral hits are a solved thing to be saturated... plenty of hidden gems made today would dwarf those two examples if they had been discovered in the same way.

replies.author: count023
replies.body: i'm just saying htat AI can level the field between a non coder and a coder in terms of game design, someone may be great on theorties and concepts and horrible at execution, now they dont have to be great at execution because hte execution phase can be automated to a degree and let them focus on the design. Undertale is a case study in "horribly executed but perfectly delivered" for isntance.

replies.author: DuckAndQwack
replies.body: Well, marketing will still be matter to make your game have more than ~30 views and 2-3 players. Nowadays the field is very saturated, so you need have not bad concept, good execution and some luck, or you have a huge risk to be unseen

replies.author: Nerodon
replies.body:
Undertale had masterful music by a guy that was popular for making homestuck music.

The game was not a complete execution disaster, because it was functional, played within its limits and the creator waa an artist with great skill.

He also used that renown to pierce into the market, had it been anyone else, its doubtful it would have gone viral.

comments.author: why_so_sergious
comments.body: as always mobile game slop will bring most money..

comments.author: fued
comments.body: I think we are going to see a glut of 'generic events' in games, and the ones who stick out are the ones who have content hand crafted

comments.author: Building-Old
comments.body: Standards are already getting lower. AI is best at making low value projects profitable due to the decreased overhead of producing uncomplicated things. Basically, where $2000 revenue used to be a non starter, now it makes sense. So, if we continue course, the most predictable thing is we will be flooded with low effort crap.

comments.author: ballbreakersgame
comments.body: I think you'll probably start to see a lot more simulation style games honestly. Art is still a pipeline blocker for games that are being pumped out with AI but simulation games dont necessarily require as much and the barrier to entry is lower since AI can write the algorithms.

replies.author: Capital-Meringue-168
replies.body:
Yeah, simulation hits a sweet spot here. The pipeline blocker moves from art to balance, and AI is way better at "tweak this coefficient, rerun a 1000-tick sim" than it is at making a coherent painting. Stuff like Rimworld and Caves of Qud already scaled by piling on rules, not assets, so iterating on systems gets a lot faster.



  


Honestly the moat just becomes whose simulation feels alive, not whose engine is fanciest.

comments.author: BAJ-JohnBen
comments.body:
Gamedev is already accessible, the problem isn't more accessibility (that is if you're not disabled in some way). The problem is 1) resources and 2) discipline and patience. 

As for ten years from now. Look at what's being made now and ask what's rising to the top? What AI-made/assisted game is pushing AI away from slop to being considered as art? AI isn't new anymore.  Just like with all forms of technology that changes art, it'll take a string of successful developers to showcase the art is still art (I have my opinions on the whole "luddite" takes in the AI space). The problem with AI is that quality VARIES far more than it did in the past. When you lower the accessibility too much, as what AI did, the tech opened far more trash and lower-quality games than in the past. So in the end, chances are, things will likely not change for AI. There will be people who'll come to show they are doing interesting stuff with AI.

comments.author: PriceMore
comments.body: Games with art and content. Ie why nobody made another Morrowind yet even though game making has been getting easier and easier since forever.

replies.author: CryAromona
replies.body: agree, art and content is the most important

comments.author: arcadezone_fun
comments.body: Honestly I think games with strong social experiences and genuinely unique gameplay will become way more valuable AI can help make games faster, but it’s a lot harder to fake creativity  community or memorable experiences people actually connect with.

comments.author: playthelastsecret
comments.body:
I guess we will see more flexible interaction with characters in games. More freedom how a plot evolves. Media content that is generated on the fly using AI and follow the individual evolution of the story thatthe player created.

We will also see more niche games that are still top quality, since production costs will go down, in particular for graphical heavy genres.

comments.author: Just-Investigator-20
comments.body:
I’m inclined to look even further ahead: within less than a decade, the vast majority of software—including video games—will be developed primarily by AI. In fact, many industries have already undergone this very transformation. Decades ago, carpentry was a purely manual trade; most practitioners needed the ability to craft a table or a chair entirely from scratch—starting with a raw tree. Nowadays, aside from certain luxury goods that deliberately emphasize their handmade nature to justify a premium price, purely manual craftsmanship is a rarity. If machinery and equipment can manufacture products that meet everyone’s needs—saving both time and effort in the process—is manual labor truly necessary anymore? Perhaps the only ones who still perceive value in it are the artisans themselves—those who possess these specific skills.



The same applies to the gaming industry; I don’t necessarily agree with the notion that "the value of these games will diminish." When humans are increasingly liberated from the rote tasks of coding and digital art creation—thereby freeing up more resources to focus on the question of "how to make this game even better"—the overall quality of games will inevitably rise. Or, as you suggested, we may see the emergence of more ambitious projects with a higher degree of creative complexity.



It’s difficult to predict with certainty... In any case, I’d love to hear your thoughts on the matter.

replies.author: FutureLynx_
replies.body: it seems your comment was created by AI. But anyways, yeah so, thats good but also sucks. what are we going to do then? it seems like then it becomes irrelevant to make games, right? These are industries together with software engineering that employ millions and millions of people. If they are all out of work, its not like our life will get better. It will get really bad. Because we will all compete for manual labour jobs that machines cant do, until machines can do them. Then what? Do we then realize we should fight the robots and their owners (billionaires), and just die? If games can be automated everything can be automated. And according to our experience in history there is no mercy for the people once a new tech arrives, we are just discarded. anyways... what do you think?

replies.author: Just-Investigator-20
replies.body: No, I wrote it by myself. But since my main language is not english, AI helped me do the translate, maybe this is the reason it read too "AI" 😞

replies.author: Just-Investigator-20
replies.body:
For the moment, I am not quite that pessimistic. However—much like how the automobile emerged to replace the horse-drawn carriage, or how automated textile mills eliminated the need for so many manual laborers—the advent of new technologies will undoubtedly displace certain roles, yet it will simultaneously give rise to new forms of employment. Since the dawn of industrialization, the general trend has been a decline in the demand for purely physical labor—or at least a reduction in its sheer volume; nevertheless, people have consistently found new, suitable occupations to pursue (or have simply gained more leisure time for recreation).

The video game industry is no exception. At the very least, AI can now handle tasks such as coding and digital art creation for us (even allowing me to simply input my thoughts in my native tongue and wait for the system to output them in English). However—at least for the time being—AI is not yet capable of designing a truly "fun" game; consequently, the time we save on coding can be redirected toward these more creative and conceptual aspects of development. I even envision a future scenario where, by simply articulating an idea to an AI, we could generate \*N\* different game prototypes in a single day for us to test and validate. "Game by Talk"—creating games through conversation—could very well prove to be a positive development. Though, perhaps, the carpenter will never again have the opportunity to craft a chair with his own two hands.
